references.text: Adam and Eve tried to cover their nakedness themselves with fig leaves, but God replaced this inadequate solution with garments of skin—an image that humanity's own attempts to cover sin are insufficient.
Abel's offering of the firstborn from his flock is the first mentioned animal sacrifice after God took an animal's life to clothe Adam and Eve, marking the beginning of the sacrificial system.
Isaiah describes how God clothes His people in a garment of salvation and a robe of righteousness—a spiritual parallel to how God clothed Adam and Eve with garments He Himself had made.
The garments of skin presupposed that an animal must die to cover human nakedness. This points forward to the biblical principle that without the shedding of blood there is no forgiveness.
Those who have washed their robes and made them white in the Lamb's blood show the final fulfillment of what God began in the Garden of Eden—covering human shame through the blood of a sacrifice.
Jesus advises the church in Laodicea to buy white garments to cover their shameful nakedness—an echo of how God covered Adam and Eve's nakedness in the Garden of Eden.
The skin garments in Eden are a foreshadowing of the principles of the law of sacrifices: sin requires an offering (life) to be covered.
Typological parallel: The skin garments anticipate that forgiveness requires an offering (life) to cover sin.
The skin garments are the first illustration that God covers sin so that it is not credited to humanity.
Typological connection: Skin (dead flesh) in Eden anticipates Christ's coming in 'the likeness of sinful flesh' to deal with sin.
The skin garments presuppose a sacrificial animal, which directly foreshadows the law's requirement for a guilt offering for sin.
